extracted.intended_audience: judges, juries, and practitioners in patent litigation (drafting/applying jury instructions)
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent litigation covering obviousness (including inherency and level of skill), enablement, written-description, and damages (lost profits, reasonable royalty, and related damages issues). Intended to guide courts, jurors, and counsel in evaluating legal standards and evidentiary factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency in Obviousness Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Something inherent from the explicit disclosure of the prior art must be limited when applied in an obviousness analysis and used only when the inherent element is the natural result of the combination of prior art elements explicitly disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An important consideration when determining whether a reference inherently discloses a previously unknown property is whether that property is unexpected. Although all properties of something are inherently part of that thing, if a property is found to be unexpectedly present, then the property may be nonobvious. (Citing KSR, Graham, Arendi, PAR Pharm., Alcon, In re Kubin.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of Ordinary Skill in the Art
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine obviousness, you must determine the level of ordinary skill in the field of the invention (at the time of the Cutoff Date). The person of ordinary skill is presumed to know all prior art you have determined reasonably relevant and is a person of ordinary creativity who can use common sense to solve problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties have agreed to the level, state their agreement. If not, consider all evidence including: (1) level of education and experience of persons actively working in the field as of the Cutoff Date (including the inventor(s)); (2) the types of problems encountered in the art and prior art solutions to those problems; and (3) the sophistication of the technology in the art as of the Cutoff Date, including the rapidity with which innovations were made. (Citing KSR, Graham, Ruiz, Envtl. Designs.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary Considerations / Objective Indicia of Nonobviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain factors may help determine whether the invention would have been obvious; no factor alone is dispositive and the obviousness of the invention must be considered as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide only instructions relevant and supported by admitted evidence. Consider whether: (1) products covered by the claim were commercially successful due to the merits of the claimed invention rather than advertising or other features; (2) there was a long-felt need satisfied by the claimed invention; (3) others tried but failed to solve the problem; (4) others copied the claimed invention; (5) the claimed invention achieved unexpectedly superior results over the closest prior art; (6) others in the field or the defendant praised the invention or expressed surprise; (7) others accepted licenses because of the merits. These factors are relevant only if there is a nexus between the consideration and the invention; the patentee bears the burden of proving nexus and admissibility. (Citing Graham, U.S. v. Adams, Apple v. Samsung, WBIP v. Kohler.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement Requirement (35 U.S.C. §112)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) ___ are invalid for lack of enablement. The Defendant bears the burden of establishing by clear and convincing evidence that the specification fails to satisfy the enablement requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent must disclose sufficient information to enable persons of ordinary skill in the field of the invention as of the effective filing date to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation. Patents are written for persons of ordinary skill, so the specification need not state information such persons would likely know. The fact that some experimentation may be required does not mean the patent is not enabled. Factors to consider for undue experimentation include: the quantity of experimentation necessary and whether that experimentation involves only known or commonly used techniques; the amount of direction or guidance disclosed in the patent; the presence or absence of working examples; the nature of the invention; the state of the prior art; the relative skill of those in the art; the predictability of the art; and the breadth of the claims. Enablement is a question of law for the Court; the jury should be instructed on subsidiary fact issues only if there are specific factual issues for the jury to decide. (Citing 35 U.S.C. §112; Amgen v. Sanofi; In re Wands.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-Description Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) ___ are invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description requirement. The Defendant bears the burden of establishing by clear and convincing evidence that the specification fails to satisfy the written-description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent must contain a written description of the product or method claimed to ensure the applicant actually invented the claimed subject matter. To satisfy the requirement, the specification must describe each and every limitation of a patent claim in sufficient detail (the exact words need not be used). The written-description requirement is satisfied if persons of ordinary skill would recognize from the specification that the inventor possessed the subject matter claimed as of the effective filing date, even if claims changed later. It is unnecessary to spell out every detail or provide specific examples, but enough must be included to convince POSA that the inventor possessed the full scope of the invention. Factors to consider include: the nature and scope of the patent claims; the complexity, predictability, and maturity of the technology; the existing knowledge in the field; and the scope and content of the prior art. Written-description sufficiency is decided claim-by-claim and is a question of fact (instruct jurors only if specific claims are challenged and there is sufficient evidentiary support). (Citing 35 U.S.C. §112; Ariad; Boston Sci.; Vas‑Cath.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages—General Principles (35 U.S.C. §284)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you find that the accused device or method infringes any asserted claims and those claims are not invalid, you must determine the amount of damages to be awarded the plaintiff for the infringement. The Plaintiff must prove each element of its damages, including amount, by a preponderance of the evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages must compensate the plaintiff for the infringement (putting the plaintiff in about the same financial position it would have been in but for the infringement). The damages award cannot be less than a reasonable royalty. Do not add anything to punish, to set an example, or for interest. The jury should address damages only if it finds one or more asserted claims both not invalid and infringed. (Citing 35 U.S.C. §284; WesternGeco; ResQNet; Aro; etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Date Damages Begin / Notice and Marking
rubrics_metrics.description: The start date for damages is either the date the plaintiff first notified the defendant of its claim (direct notice) or the date the plaintiff effectively provided public notice by marking substantially all products with the patent number (including virtual marking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If parties stipulate the start date, use it. For public notice by marking: marking substantially all products with the patent number or marking with a freely accessible internet address that connects the product with the patent number suffices; licensees must also mark. Public marking is effective even if the defendant did not see it. Direct notice starts from the date the defendant received it. If the plaintiff did not provide effective public mark or direct notice before filing suit, the plaintiff can only recover damages for infringement after it sued (with a practice note that if no patented products were ever made/offered/sold—e.g., only method claims—plaintiff can recover up to six years before filing suit even without notice). (Citing 35 U.S.C. §§286, 287(a); Arctic Cat; Funai; Gart; etc.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of Damages Available
rubrics_metrics.description: There are several kinds of damages available for patent infringement, principally lost profits and a reasonable royalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lost profits compensate the patentee for additional profits it would have made 'but for' the infringement, including related collateral product losses or price effects in appropriate circumstances. A reasonable royalty is the amount a willing licensee would have paid and a patentee would have accepted just before infringement began; it is the minimum amount recoverable. (Citing 35 U.S.C. §284; historic cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost Profits—'But For' Test
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove lost profits, the plaintiff must show that but for the defendant's infringement, the plaintiff would have made additional profits through the sale of all or a portion of the sales of the allegedly infringing products made by the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove lost profits by a preponderance of the evidence. The jury must determine what purchasers would have done if the alleged infringement had not occurred. The profits referenced are those allegedly lost by the plaintiff, not profits made by the defendant on infringing sales. (Citing Am. Seating; Aro; Ericsson; Tate Access Floors.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factors for Lost Profits
rubrics_metrics.description: The plaintiff proves lost profits by showing each of the following factors by a preponderance: (1) demand for the patented product in the relevant market; (2) absence of acceptable non-infringing substitutes; (3) plaintiff's manufacturing and marketing ability to make the sales; and (4) the amount of profit the plaintiff would have made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the plaintiff proves each Panduit factor, it is entitled to lost profits. The instruction explains each factor in detail in subsequent subsections. (Citing Mentor Graphics; Rite‑Hite; Panduit Corp.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor—Demand for the Patented Product/Method
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove demand in the relevant market by showing significant sales of the plaintiff's own patented product/method or demand for a product/method that directly competes with the defendant's infringing product/method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To use defendant's sales as proof, the plaintiff's and defendant's products must be sufficiently similar to compete in the same market or market segment. Evidence of significant sales of the defendant's covered products can establish demand if products compete. (Citing DePuy Spine; BIC Leisure.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor—Acceptable Non‑Infringing Substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether non-infringing acceptable substitutes competed with the defendant's infringing product in the marketplace and what impact those substitutes would have had absent the defendant's sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An acceptable substitute must have had one or more advantages of the patented invention important to actual buyers and must not infringe (either licensed or lacking required features). It may be a modified version of the infringing product that avoids infringement. The substitute must have been available during the damages period (need not have actually been sold). If not sold during the damages period, defendant must show by a preponderance that a competitor or defendant had necessary equipment/materials/know-how to design and manufacture it. If some customers would likely have bought substitutes, plaintiff is not entitled to lost profits for those sales. Even if no substitutes had the advantages of the patented invention, plaintiff still must prove it would have made the defendant's sales. (Citing Presidio Components; DePuy Spine; Grain Processing; Standard Havens; SmithKline.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor—Market Share Allocation When Substitutes Exist
rubrics_metrics.description: If acceptable non-infringing substitutes existed, plaintiff may recover lost profits for a portion of defendant's infringing sales based on plaintiff's market share.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove it more likely than not that its product competed in the same market and that it would have made a portion of the infringing sales equal to at least its share of that market but for the defendant's infringement. It is not necessary to prove the plaintiff and defendant were the only suppliers in the market. (Citing DePuy Spine; Ericsson; Crystal Semiconductor; BIC Leisure; State Indus.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor—Capacity (Manufacturing and Marketing Ability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff must prove it had the manufacturing and marketing ability to actually make the sales it allegedly lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must show it could have supplied the additional products needed for the sales, or that someone working with plaintiff could have, and must show it more likely than not had the ability to market and sell these additional products. (Citing Wechsler; Fonar; Datascope; Gyromat.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor—Amount of Profit (Incremental Income Approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may calculate lost profits by calculating lost sales and subtracting additional costs/expenses that plaintiff would have incurred to make the lost sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The amount of lost profits cannot be speculative but need not be proven with unerring certainty. Use incremental income approach where appropriate. (Citing Kalman; King Instrument; Paper Converting; Bio‑Rad; Lam.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Price Erosion Damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff may recover additional damages if but for the defendant's infringement, plaintiff would have charged higher prices or would not have had to lower its prices for its products/methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If plaintiff meets burden, award additional damages equal to difference between profits at higher price and profits actually made at lower price. If using the higher price in calculating lost sales and lost profits, account for any decrease in plaintiff's sales that might have occurred due to the higher price. (Citing Siemens Med. Sols.; Ericsson; Vulcan; Rite‑Hite; BIC Leisure; Lam.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost Escalation Damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff can recover additional damages for increased costs (e.g., additional marketing costs) that it incurred because of the defendant's infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove it is more likely than not that its costs increased because of the defendant's actions and not for some other reason. (Citing Amstar; Lam.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Convoyed Sales (Collateral Products) Damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff contends its product is ordinarily sold along with collateral products; plaintiff may seek damages for lost sales of collateral products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To recover lost profits for collateral products, plaintiff must prove (1) it is more likely than not that it would have sold the collateral products but for the infringement; and (2) the collateral products and the product/method are so closely related that they act or are used together for a common purpose. Damages for collateral sales are calculated like lost profits for the main product. (Citing DePuy Spine; Rite‑Hite; State Indus.; Paper Converting.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—General
rubrics_metrics.description: If plaintiff has not proven lost profits (or only proven for part of the sales), the plaintiff is entitled to a reasonable royalty for the remaining infringing sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reasonable royalty must be enough to compensate for the infringement but no less than the amount that would have been agreed in a hypothetical negotiation just before the infringement began. The award must reflect the incremental value the patented invention adds to the end product and must allocate value between patented and unpatented features—no more than the value attributable to infringing features. (Citing 35 U.S.C. §284; Power Integrations; Exmark; Ericsson v. D‑Link; VirnetX; Apple v. Motorola; Uniloc; Lucent.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable Royalty—Hypothetical Negotiation Method
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable royalty is the royalty that would have resulted from a hypothetical license negotiation between the plaintiff and defendant, assuming they negotiated just before the infringement began and both parties believed the patent was valid and infringed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume both parties had full knowledge of the facts and circumstances surrounding the infringement at the hypothetical negotiation. Use this hypothetical negotiation framework to determine the royalty base and rate. (Citing Apple v. Motorola; LaserDynamics; Uniloc; Fujifilm; Lucent; Maxwell; Rite‑Hite; Wang Labs.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors Relevant to Reasonable Royalty (Hypothetical Negotiation)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining a reasonable royalty, the jury may consider evidence on various economic and licensing factors relevant to the hypothetical negotiation, in addition to any other evidence of the patent's economic value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider only factors relevant and supported by admitted evidence. Possible factors include: (1) any royalties received by the licensor proving an established royalty; (2) rates paid by defendant to license comparable patents; (3) nature and scope of the license (exclusive/nonexclusive, territorial restrictions); (4) licensor's policy/program to preserve exclusivity; (5) commercial relationship between licensor and licensee (competitors or not); (6) effect of selling the patented product in promoting other sales and extent of collateral sales; (7) duration of the patent and term of the license; (8) established profitability, commercial success, and popularity of the product; (9) utility and advantages of the patented invention over prior modes/devices; (10) nature and character of the patented invention and commercial embodiment and benefits to users; (11) extent to which defendant has made use of the invention and evidence of value of that use; (12) portion of profit or selling price customary in the business to allow for use of the invention; (13) portion of profit arising from the patented invention as opposed to unpatented features; (14) opinion testimony of qualified experts; (15) the amount that a licensor and licensee would have agreed upon at the time infringement began (what a prudent licensee would pay and a willing patentee accept); and (16) any other economic factor a normally prudent business person would consider in negotiating the hypothetical license. (List only those factors relevant and supported by evidence.)
